title: Tashkent Rising
premise: Edmund Sandoval, a translator for a doomed peace delegation in Tashkent, has spent years cultivating mediocrity as camouflage. When a stranger named Varga repays a favor Edmund never performed—delivering him a coded ledger and a debt—he is pulled into an extraction plot centered on Ilkhom Rakhimov, a defector carrying proof that the peace talks themselves are a laundering scheme for stolen state funds. Edmund discovers the defector is bait: the talks' host, Minister Karimov, intends to let the extraction proceed only to kill everyone aboard and bury the evidence with them. Edmund must choose between his polished invisibility and the one act of visibility that could save the flight—exposing himself and the ledger at dawn, trading his anonymity for survival and a conscience he can no longer silence.
about_author: E. M. Ashgrove is the pen name of a former NGO field coordinator who spent six years across Central Asia before turning to fiction. Ashgrove writes thrillers about people whose jobs are to be forgotten.

chapters.title: The Packed Bag
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. We meet him mid-delegation: fluent, forgettable, translating platitudes between men who have already decided to fail. He checks his go-bag under the hotel bed, rehearses his exit story, and notes the new security man watching him too closely. Emotional beat: the comfort of invisibility, already fraying.

chapters.title: A Favor Returned
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. A stranger, Varga, corners him in a tea house and repays a favor from a name Edmund once used years ago—a favor he never did. The payment: a coded ledger implicating the peace process itself, and a message: interest is owed. Emotional beat: vertigo; his careful identity has a past he doesn't recognize.

chapters.title: The Defector
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Varga explains the job: get Ilkhom Rakhimov, a senior auditor turned defector, onto a dawn charter flight out of a military airfield outside the city. Edmund refuses, then finds the ledger's cipher keyed to his old alias—someone built this trap around him specifically. Emotional beat: dread hardening into reluctant resolve.

chapters.title: Minister Karimov's Table
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Edmund translating at a banquet where Minister Karimov delivers a speech about trust, while his security chief, Doston, quietly reroutes airfield credentials. Edmund realizes Karimov knows about the flight—and is letting it happen. Emotional beat: the sick clarity of watching a trap being set politely.

chapters.title: Ilkhom
chapters.summary: Ilkhom's POV. Hiding in a safehouse, the defector reflects on what he stole and why—not money, but the arithmetic of theft itself. He suspects he is bait and goes anyway, because his daughter's exit visa dies at dawn too. Emotional beat: fatalism laced with love; the price of survival made personal.

chapters.title: Interest Owed
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Varga reveals the truth: the original 'favor' was committed by the real owner of Edmund's alias, now dead—and the ledger was always meant to reach Karimov through whoever carried it. Edmund understands he is disposable packaging. He decides to turn the delivery into leverage instead. Emotional beat: anger converting fear into agency.

chapters.title: Credentials
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Edmund trades a fragment of the ledger to Doston for airfield access, lying beautifully in two languages; meanwhile Ilkhom moves through checkpoint Tashkent with forged papers, each guard a coin flip. Emotional beat: the intoxicating and corrupting ease of Edmund's first real betrayal of his own neutrality.

chapters.title: The Airfield at Night
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. On the tarmac, Edmund sees the refueling truck that shouldn't be there and the second security detail that isn't Varga's—the flight is meant to burn. He gets Ilkhom and his daughter aboard early and cuts the fuel line, buying minutes with sabotage. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into decisiveness.

chapters.title: Dawn
chapters.summary: Climax. Multiple POVs converge: Doston's kill team arrives, Varga turns out to be playing his own government's angle, and Edmund chooses visibility—broadcasting the ledger's contents over the airfield radio and to the delegation, making himself the story no one can quietly erase. The plane lifts through ground fire as Karimov's machine begins devouring its own. Emotional beat: the terrible freedom of having nothing left to hide behind.

chapters.title: What Survival Costs
chapters.summary: Resolution. Weeks later, Edmund testifies from an unnamed European capital; the peace process collapses publicly, exactly as it was always going to, but honestly now. Ilkhom rebuilds in exile; Varga vanishes, debts presumably settled. Edmund unpacks the go-bag at last and leaves it empty. Emotional beat: grief and relief braided together—the inheritance he finally accepts is his own name.
